tales.title: The Knight’s Tale
tales.voice: A seasoned soldier brings the company a grand romance of rivalry, ceremony and uncertain fortune.
tales.premise: Two imprisoned cousins see Emelye from their window and become rivals. Their story unfolds in an imagined ancient Athens, where human plans must contend with the gods.
tales.note: War, imprisonment, fatal injury and women’s restricted choices.
tales.question: Whose wishes count when a romance makes a woman the prize?
reveal: Theseus arranges a tournament to decide whether Palamon or Arcite will marry Emelye. The three pray for different things: Palamon for love, Arcite for victory, and Emelye to remain unmarried—or, failing that, to marry the man who loves her most.

Arcite wins, but an accident fatally injures him. After mourning and the passage of time, Theseus arranges Emelye’s marriage to Palamon. The ending establishes peace while leaving readers room to question the price of that order.
tales.alt: Imagined tournament garden in ancient Athens, with rival knights and a woman among patterned trees and banners

tales.title: The Miller’s Tale
tales.voice: An intoxicated interrupter answers the Knight’s noble romance with an outrageous Oxford household comedy.
tales.premise: A jealous carpenter, his young wife, a clever student and an eager parish clerk have very different ideas about love. Nobody has quite the control they imagine.
tales.note: Adult sexual and scatological humor, unwanted sexual touching, adultery and injury.
tales.question: When everyone is trying to be clever, who gets to tell the final version?
reveal: Nicholas persuades John that another great flood is coming, so John hangs tubs from the roof as makeshift boats. While John sleeps in his tub, Nicholas and Alisoun meet downstairs. At the window, Alisoun gives her other admirer, Absolon, a humiliating substitute for a kiss.

Absolon returns with a hot plough blade. Nicholas receives the burn and shouts for water; John thinks the flood has arrived, cuts his rope and falls. His neighbors accept the lovers’ account that he is mad. The comedy’s victory depends on someone else’s pain and public humiliation.

source.title: Harvard: The Miller’s Prologue and Tale
source.lineRange: Fragment I, lines 3109–3854; unwanted touching at 3276–3287

tales.alt: Imagined moonlit timber house with a carpenter, student and candlelit window in the Miller’s Oxford comedy

tales.title: The Wife of Bath’s Tale
tales.voice: A widely traveled woman with five marriages insists that lived experience deserves a hearing.
tales.premise: In an Arthurian setting, a knight who has raped a woman faces judgment. The queen gives him a year and a day to discover what women most desire.
tales.note: Rape, coercive marriage, misogyny; domestic abuse in the accompanying prologue.
tales.question: Can someone learn to respect another person’s choices without controlling the answer?
reveal: An older woman supplies the answer: women want power within relationships, rather than to be ruled by husbands or lovers. In return, the knight has promised to do what she asks; she asks him to marry her. When he rejects her age, appearance and social standing, she challenges his ideas about what makes a person noble.

She offers him a choice about her appearance and fidelity. He leaves the decision to her, and the tale rewards that surrender of control with a transformation and a happy marriage. That resolution does not erase the assault that began the story or tell us what happened to its victim.

source.title: Harvard: The Wife of Bath’s Prologue and Tale
source.lineRange: Fragment III, prologue 1–856; tale 857–1264; rape at 887–888

tales.alt: Symbolic scene combining the Wife of Bath as storyteller, a mirror, an Arthurian castle and an older wise woman

tales.title: The Nun’s Priest’s Tale
tales.voice: A priest accompanying the Prioress makes a farmyard sound as consequential as an epic battlefield.
tales.premise: Chanticleer, a magnificent rooster, has a disturbing dream. His companion Pertelote disputes its meaning, while a fox waits for the right moment to flatter him.
tales.note: Animal peril, sexual innuendo and misogynistic claims voiced and qualified by the storyteller.
tales.question: What happens when a compliment sounds better than a warning?
reveal: The fox praises Chanticleer’s singing and persuades him to close his eyes and stretch his neck. The fox seizes him, sending the widow’s household into a noisy chase.

Chanticleer turns speech into an escape tool: he suggests that the fox taunt the pursuers. When the fox opens his mouth, the rooster flies free. Both creatures have been tricked by words, and the storyteller offers several lessons rather than one tidy answer.
tales.alt: Chanticleer the rooster and a watchful fox in a vividly painted farmyard

tales.title: The Pardoner’s Tale
tales.voice: A preacher boasts about exploiting his listeners, then delivers a powerful warning against greed.
tales.premise: Three young revelers set out to kill Death. A mysterious old man points them toward a tree, where their search takes an unexpected turn.
tales.note: Murder, poisoning, death, drunkenness and religious exploitation.
tales.question: Can a dishonest storyteller tell a story that is true about us?
reveal: Under the tree they find gold. They send the youngest to buy provisions while the other two plot to murder him and keep his share. He independently buys poison to kill them.

They stab him when he returns, then drink the poisoned wine and die. After demonstrating what greed can do, the Pardoner tries to sell his own wares to the company. The Host’s furious response exposes the gap between the sermon and its salesman.

source.title: Harvard: The Pardoner’s Prologue, Introduction, and Tale
source.lineRange: Fragment VI, prologue 329–462; tale and concluding exchange 463–968

tales.alt: Three revelers approach gold beneath a great oak in an imagined forest; a shadow hints at danger

tales.title: The Franklin’s Tale
tales.voice: A prosperous landowner associated with generous hospitality asks what generosity might cost.
tales.premise: On the coast of Brittany, Dorigen worries about her absent husband and the rocks that threaten his ship. An unwelcome suitor hears what she thinks is an impossible condition.
tales.note: Sexual pressure, suicidal thoughts and references to rape and suicide in classical examples.
tales.question: Is keeping a promise always the right thing to do?
reveal: Dorigen says she will accept Aurelius’s love if he removes the coastal rocks. A learned magician makes the rocks seem to disappear, and Aurelius presses her to honor the promise. Dorigen is distraught; her husband Arveragus insists that she keep her word.

Aurelius releases her rather than demand fulfillment. The magician, hearing what happened, cancels Aurelius’s enormous fee. The Franklin asks his listeners to judge who was most generous. Readers can also ask how the men’s exchange of generosity accounts for Dorigen’s freedom.

source.title: Harvard: The Franklin’s Prologue and Tale
source.lineRange: Fragment V, tale 729–1624; Dorigen’s distress and examples at 1355–1456

tales.alt: Dorigen looks from a Breton coast toward the sea, with jagged rocks and an imagined clear horizon

routes.label: Wit with a sting
routes.description: Begin with a fox’s compliment, then meet a preacher who knows exactly how words work.

routes.label: Who gets to choose?
routes.description: Two tales put authority, marriage and the cost of a promise under pressure. Read their content notes first.

routes.label: A romance, answered
routes.description: Hear the Knight’s grand story, then the Miller’s unruly reply. The second stop brings adult humor.

connections.title: Who gets the last word?
connections.body: The Wife’s tale asks who should hold authority in marriage. The Franklin’s asks what happens when promises and generosity determine someone else’s choices. Where do you hear freedom—and where do you hear pressure?

connections.title: When does persuasion become a trap?
connections.body: A fox performs admiration; a Pardoner performs moral authority. Both understand their listeners’ desires. Compare the claims a listener is invited to trust before opening either ending.

connections.title: What changes when the setting changes?
connections.body: The Knight’s rival lovers inhabit an elevated world of ceremony. The Miller’s inhabit a crowded Oxford household. His interruption is a reply inside the frame: how do status, voice and the audience’s laughter change a love story?

journey.title: Southwark · the Tabard
journey.body: The fictional company gathers at the Tabard Inn in Southwark. Harry Bailey proposes a contest: two tales each on the outward journey and two on the return, with a meal for the winner.

journey.title: Rochester · the road through Kent
journey.body: Rochester is a real anchor on scholarly reconstructions of the road to Canterbury. Our illustrated journey is a schematic: it does not fix the company’s exact itinerary or place these six tales at particular stops.

journey.title: Story worlds · beyond the road
journey.body: A tale can leave Kent behind: ancient Athens, Oxford, Arthurian Britain, a widow’s farmyard, Flanders, coastal Brittany. These are the stories’ imagined settings, not stops on the pilgrimage or pins on a historical map.

journey.title: Canterbury · the intended destination
journey.body: The pilgrims seek Thomas Becket’s shrine at Canterbury Cathedral. Chaucer’s surviving work never completes the announced contest or the return journey. Our arrival scene imagines the destination, rather than supplying a missing ending.

lines.middle: Thanne longen folk to goon on pilgrimages,
lines.gloss: At that time, people feel the pull of a pilgrim journey.

lines.middle: Of Engelond to Caunterbury they wende,
lines.gloss: From across England, they make their way to Canterbury.
They intended to travel on horseback toward Canterbury.

lines.middle: Trouthe and honour, fredom and curteisie.
lines.gloss: The Knight valued faithfulness, honor, generosity and courteous conduct.
